items.title: Amid worldwide doomsday prepping, NATO publicly shared its resilience requirements for the first time—including stockpiling blood, food, and water
items.summary:
Governments seem to be battening down the hatches on a global scale, and amid it all, NATO updated its resilience requirements for member countries to prepare for a “sustained crisis.” 

In its updated 2026 baseline requirements, NATO told its member countries to prepare everything they needed for the safety and well-being of citizens in the event of a crisis—and the ability to manage a “mass influx” of people from a secure government headquarters.

Baseline requirements from NATO have circulated for the past decade, but in 2026 they were shared publicly for the first time. NATO said its aim in doing so is to “[broaden] its resilience community and [build] a common understanding of our resilience efforts.”

It came just days before the Pentagon launched an initiative at the end of September called FORTRESS , which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains. 

Then, in late October, the U.K. government released a prepping checklist of items households should stockpile to “stay prepared if everyday services are temporarily disrupted.” The advice is part of a three-year campaign to ensure preparedness, the U.K. government said, and asked households to keep items such as cash, bottled water and pet food in stock.

NATO’s most recent advice is similarly striking. Its objectives for member countries—including the U.S., U.K., Canada, and Germany—include having infrastructure in place for national defense and governmental continuity, including a resilient (“both environmentally and…
items.t: Amid worldwide doomsday prepping, NATO publicly shared its resilience requirements for the first time—including stockpiling blood, food, and water

items.title: Jensen Huang says he ‘would be honored’ to return as CEO in first statement since resigning from Nvidia
items.summary:
Hours before Nvidia reports its first quarterly results without him, and with reports swirling that a Sam Altman-style resurrection is desired in some areas of Silicon Valley, Jensen Huang told the board he’s available to come back if they want.

In his first statement since he resigned last week, the former CEO said he would love to return to the company, but only if its board asked him to. The company has lost $450 billion in market value since he admitted the affair, and a person familiar told CNBC on Monday the board isn’t considering bringing him back while it runs a national security investigation into his conduct.

“Since my departure, I’ve seen an outpouring of calls from NVIDIA’s employees, investors, business partners, and customers for me to return as CEO,” Huang wrote in a post on X late Tuesday morning. 

“If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.”

In the post, Huang said he erred in his personal life and “created problems” for everyone involved. He wrote that he owns his mistakes and will cooperate with the board’s independent investigation.

“I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life. I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely.”

Huang’s resignation 

Huang resigned Thursday, ending 33 years as CEO. Days earlier, after he admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. intelligence…
items.t: Jensen Huang says he ‘would be honored’ to return as CEO in first statement since resigning from Nvidia

items.title: Exclusive: Cognition bets on ‘Devin Bots’ coding agents in challenge to Anthropic’s Duet and OpenAI’s Dots
items.summary:
Cognition’s AI coder just got promoted. The startup, currently valued at $48 billion, helped kick off the race to build coding agents with its viral product Devin. Now it is trying to get back to the front of the pack by debuting Devin Bots, a persistent coding tool that acts as a manager for teams of Devin agents that can manage a complex project over days or even weeks. 

In the past few months, several AI companies have rolled out always-on agents that are designed to be general-purpose, but can be used for coding tasks. OpenAI has unveiled Dots, an always-on proactive agent that integrates with its Codex product to run teams of agents handling software development tasks. Anthropic has unveiled a similar product called Duet that can integrate with its Claude Code product.

But Cognition’s Devin Bots are some of the first to be designed specifically for software development. 

Tell a Bot to build an Android version of your iPhone app, and it will divide up the work, assign it to Devin agents and keep the Android app updated as the iPhone version changes. “Self-driving software is, I think, the direction that it’s going,” CEO Scott Wu told Fortune at the company’s office in San Francisco’s SoMa neighborhood. “But of course, it’s always up to the human where we’re driving to.”

Devin Bots is Wu’s bet that the smarter AI models get, the more the product built around them matters. His argument addresses a broader Silicon Valley debate over whether advances in AI models will squeeze out the companies building products on top of them. Wu disagrees with the idea that AI will…
items.t: Exclusive: Cognition bets on ‘Devin Bots’ coding agents in challenge to Anthropic’s Duet and OpenAI’s Dots

items.title: The Trump White House is starting to admit that your bank account and airline tickets are under attack from rogue AI
items.summary:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin went on Fox News Monday night with a theory for the week of breakdowns that grounded flights, knocked out Outlook and slowed Chase accounts: artificial intelligence. The failures came in five days. Microsoft had a worldwide outage on Thursday, Nov. 12, hitting Outlook, Teams and Exchange Online. On Friday, the FAA grounded flights across the country for only the second time since 9/11.

Then came Monday. JPMorgan Chase’s systems were disrupted for hours , hitting online banking, payments and some customer transactions, and Downdetector reports for Chase neared 5,000. Customers of Bank of America , Wells Fargo and US Bank also reported delays on transactions involving Chase.

Mullin’s source was a tech-industry contact he wouldn’t name. “I believe that it’s the SI,” Mullin told Sean Hannity, referring to “super intelligence,” the administration’s preferred term for AI. Mullin said the contact’s theory was that programs that write code and fix themselves could overwhelm systems that can’t keep up with the technology’s speed. Mullin made a point of saying the source was not Elon Musk.

In the same interview, Mullin played the threat down. He said he could tell Americans “with 98% certainty, we’re not seeing a cyber attack” and called the incidents “all individually unrelated.”

Gary Marcus, the NYU professor emeritus and AI critic who writes the Substack Marcus on AI , has warned about this for years, and he counted the interview as a turning point. Marcus wrote Tuesday that Mullin finally broke ranks and acknowledged on Fox that…
items.t: The Trump White House is starting to admit that your bank account and airline tickets are under attack from rogue AI

items.title: The internet was built for Netflix streaming down to your couch. AT&T’s COO says AI agents are flipping it the other way
items.summary:
For two decades, the internet has mostly run one way: down. Netflix , YouTube and everything else stream from a data center to a couch, and the networks were built to match. AT&T’s chief operating officer says AI is starting to change that.

“The actual direction of the bandwidth of the internet is undergoing a fundamental shift,” Jeff McElfresh said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit. With agentic AI, he said, “we’re seeing agents tap the network in a 24 by seven, a very different approach. It’s not so episodic anymore.”

U.S. household upload traffic grew 19.2% year-over-year in the second quarter, more than three times as fast as downloads, which grew 6.1%, according to OpenVault , which tracks broadband usage for internet providers. The average subscriber now uploads 58.2 GB a month. Households still download about 11x as much as they upload, but that ratio was 16.6x in 2019. For the companies spending hundreds of billions on AI and the networks that carry it, that matters: a lot of last-mile infrastructure was built on the assumption that people mostly watch, not send.

‘There’s the Netflix traffic’ 

McElfresh has been at AT&T for 31 years. He said watching traffic from the network’s control center used to be easy to read, like “Oh wow, there’s the Netflix traffic. Oh, there’s the YouTube traffic.” Human habits created clear patterns, like traffic leaving cities for the suburbs at the start of the pandemic, when many work-from-home networks struggled and video calls glitched.

AI, he said, is “a very different approach.” Agents run around the clock…
items.t: The internet was built for Netflix streaming down to your couch. AT&T’s COO says AI agents are flipping it the other way

items.title: The man who sold Aetna to CVS for almost $70 billion says the deal was cover for problems ‘they never really fixed’—just as CVS breaks itself in two
items.summary:
Mark Bertolini sold Aetna to CVS Health for almost $70 billion in 2018. On Monday, he told a room of Fortune 500 executives what he thinks CVS was really buying.

“The real intention” of the purchase, Bertolini said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit, “was just to take the earning stream and revenue stream from [Aetna] to hide a bunch of other things that they never really fixed.” He tied that directly to the breakup CVS is going through now: “You’d never do that deal now.”

The comments land two weeks after CVS said it will split in two . CVS Health will keep Aetna and its Caremark pharmacy benefit manager and spin off its roughly 9,000 stores and MinuteClinic as a separate company, CVS Pharmacy, by the first half of 2028. CVS shares closed down 12.5% on Nov. 4, the day of the announcement, wiping out nearly $15 billion in market value. 

For employers, insurers, and anyone with a pharmacy benefit, it’s the partial unwinding of the biggest bet on vertical integration in American health care.

CVS declined to comment on Bertolini’s remarks. “This is the right decision, at the right time,” CVS Health spokesperson David Whitrap said of the split in an email to Fortune, adding that the company is “getting ahead of the external market dynamics from a position of strength. Each of our businesses are thriving.” He confirmed that Aetna and Caremark will stay together and that the separation should be finished by mid-2028.

Where’s the queen? 

Bertolini ran Aetna from 2011 through the sale and has been CEO of Oscar Health since April 2023. He had been asked by Fortune…
items.t: The man who sold Aetna to CVS for almost $70 billion says the deal was cover for problems ‘they never really fixed’—just as CVS breaks itself in two

items.title: Stryker CEO Kevin Lobo says robots now do 2 of every 3 knee replacements—and he won’t build them in China because ‘the IP is a massive worry’
items.summary:
Stryker builds every one of its orthopedic surgery robots in the U.S. CEO Kevin Lobo says it will stay that way, because of what’s happening in China.

“We have no plans to make any robots in China. The IP is a massive worry,” Lobo said Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit. “They are knocking off a lot of the other robots.”

Robots are now central to how Stryker sells joint replacements. Lobo said two of every three Stryker knee replacements are now done robotically, using its Mako system, which has been used in 2.5 million procedures in 47 countries. That makes the robot’s intellectual property a big part of what Stryker is selling. Meanwhile, Chinese makers are scaling quickly. MicroPort MedBot, a Shanghai company that makes a soft-tissue surgical robot called Toumai, said in June that it had passed 300 global orders, was installed in more than 60 countries, and could build up to 500 robots a year.

Lobo, who is Stryker’s chair and CEO, said one of Stryker’s “major competitors” had bought into a Chinese robotics company. He didn’t say which one.

‘Very thoughtful about not making anything there’ 

Fortune ’s Andrew Nusca asked the panel what role the U.S. race with China plays in robotics: talent, intellectual property or supply chains. Lobo said Stryker makes its robots at home and ships them around the world.

Stryker is “scouring the market” to see whether Chinese companies can develop new kinds of robots for other parts of the anatomy, he said. He argued that engineering talent isn’t enough in his field without clinical experience. “They can have the…
items.t: Stryker CEO Kevin Lobo says robots now do 2 of every 3 knee replacements—and he won’t build them in China because ‘the IP is a massive worry’

Over the past week, I’ve been overwhelmed by the love and support of friends, industry colleagues, and people I’ve never met. Thank you to everyone who has shown kindness to my family and me. It means the world to me.

I came to the United States 53 years ago, and becoming an American citizen is one of the greatest gifts and proudest moments of my life. NVIDIA has been my life’s work. Building it into the company it is today alongside my colleagues has been a privilege and an honor. Nowhere but in America could a company like NVIDIA be possible. items.title: Sesame Workshop CEO says you’ll never see an AI-powered Elmo toy: ‘We could have made a lot of money … but we’re just not going to do that’
items.summary:
More AI-powered tools and toys are now within the reach of young children, but consumers shouldn’t expect to see the likeness of Sesame Street characters among them.

Sesame Workshop president and CEO Sherrie Westin said at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit on Monday that the nonprofit television production company behind Sesame Street would not produce AI-powered toys that look like its characters out of concern it would get in the way of a young child connecting with their parents. It’s part of a larger framework from the nonprofit that doesn’t eschew AI entirely, but seeks out guardrails so that it can augment, not hinder young children’s education.

“We decided we will absolutely not do AI-powered anthropomorphic toys because for a young child, if we’re making Elmo AI-powered, that really runs a risk of competing with the important connection between adult and child,” Westin told Fortune AI editor Jeremy Kahn. “That’s where the real learning happens, and having something at that age, we believe, would be detrimental.” 

New plush toys, like Curio’s Gabbo , are AI-powered dolls intended for children under three. They use chatbot technology, including from OpenAI, to talk back to their child owners and were designed as a screen-free alternative for youngsters. Early research from the University of Cambridge published earlier this year found that while some practitioners believe these toys could support language and communication development, they also don’t have adept social and pretend-play capabilities, and risk misunderstanding or communicating…
items.t: Sesame Workshop CEO says you’ll never see an AI-powered Elmo toy: ‘We could have made a lot of money … but we’re just not going to do that’

items.title: Siemens and Mercedes-Benz employ 60,000-plus Americans. Their U.S. chiefs have one ask: stability
items.summary:
Mercedes-Benz set up its first U.S. manufacturing plant more than a century ago for one reason, according to Jason Hoff, the automaker’s North America CEO: to avoid tariffs. Even then, he said, “tariffs played an interesting role.”

The German carmaker is once again expanding in the U.S. with tariffs in mind, and fellow German industrial giant Siemens is investing heavily too. Speaking on Monday at the Fortune 500 Innovation Forum in Detroit , the U.S. chiefs of both companies told me what they need most from federal, state, and local governments isn’t any single policy. It’s stability.

“Stability in the regulatory environment is, I think, imperative,” said Ann Fairchild, president and CEO of Siemens USA, because “it gives companies the confidence to be able to invest for the long term.”

The two companies have real money riding on that confidence. Siemens has more than 50,000 U.S. employees and has invested more than $1 billion in U.S. manufacturing over the past five years , with more than $200 million announced since for new factories in Georgia and Texas. Fairchild said Siemens also spent $15 billion last year acquiring U.S. software companies, including Dotmatics , to build out its industrial AI business.

Mercedes-Benz, which has said it directly employs more than 11,000 people in the U.S., said in March it would invest $4 billion in its Alabama plant through 2030 , part of more than $7 billion it plans to put into U.S. operations. Hoff said the company invests more than $1 billion a year in its manufacturing facilities and other sites.

Both companies are part of a…

items.title: U.S. labor force may come to resemble China’s army of one-man companies due to AI, says Bill Gross—leveling wealth inequality and national debt
items.summary:
Though more than six in 10 Americans want to run their own companies, many just don’t know where to start. Serial entrepreneur Bill Gross has got more than a million business concepts ready to launch, and he’s sharing them for free.

Gross is the founder of Idealab, one of the longest-running tech incubators, launched in 1996, with 45 IPOs and acquisitions to its credit. Gross, who made his fortune building software, has since launched Idealab.ai—an AI-powered platform providing startup ideas, support, and investment.

The founder of education software provider Knowledge Adventure has set some tough targets for success: He wants to create 100 million jobs, countering the expected wave of AI job losses using the very technology that displaced workers. Gross believes a boom in American entrepreneurship could help offset wealth inequality and macroeconomic headwinds, such as the growing national debt.

“I had this dream of making a million companies,” Gross tells Fortune on the sidelines of the Web Summit conference in Lisbon. “I was pitching this to a group of investors, and they told me that China has 30 million one-person companies. 

“I think we could have 30 million one-person companies in the United States, and if you had 30 million one-person companies, that would really do a lot for taxation. That would do a lot for income equality, and that would do a lot for not having people near the bottom worried about where they stand relative to the people at the top.” 

AI can be used as a “leveling tool,” Gross adds: “I hope there could be 30 million companies that are very…
items.t: U.S. labor force may come to resemble China’s army of one-man companies due to AI, says Bill Gross—leveling wealth inequality and national debt

items.title: Can this experimental orchard save the UK’s cider industry?

Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests

On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.

Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

items.title: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job? | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
The Claude AI developer’s unique setup is supposedly high-minded, but still represents extraordinary power concentration

Boardroom governance matters, even in the world of big tech, it turns out. The business of how companies are run, investors are discovering, can be more complicated than handing the founder or superstar chief executive as much control as he wants (it’s usually a he) and waiting for brilliant returns to appear. Sometimes a few checks on power are useful, especially when a crisis strikes.

This revelation is no revelation at all, of course. For about 30 years until the first generation of big US tech companies came along, the thrust of corporate governance thinking was to insist on the basic fairness of the principle of “one share, one vote”. The owners should be able to chuck out misbehaving or underperforming managers by a simple majority, in other words.

Continue reading...
items.t: Anthropic recognises the risks to humanity – but is its governance really up to the job?

items.title: Milburn’s historic report on Britain’s lost generation says one key thing: finally, young lives will really matter | Polly Toynbee
items.summary:
The year-long Neets inquiry has yielded a slew of new policies. But what matters is the political and social priority shift designed to change this country

This week marks a monumental turning point for young people in Britain: finally they will come first, not last. It will mark an end, we must hope, to a perverse system that casts down the future generation and overrewards the already privileged old.

There are 1 million Neets (16- to 24-year-olds not in education, employment or training) in the UK, and they are partly George Osborne’s progeny. He targeted the young, tearing down the Connexions youth service, careers guidance, youth clubs, family benefits and further education funding. Michael Gove, with his Gradgrind exam fixation, scythed through music, sports, arts, drama and technology – subjects that kept many engaged with school. Remember the playing fields sold, the leisure centres closed, the mental health services for…
